newsitem.title: USA: Collector turns passion for coins into lucrative career.
newsitem.headline: Collector turns passion for coins into lucrative career.

text.p: Like most children growing up in south Philadelphia, Silvano Di Genova played street games and cared little for coins. Then he found an old piggy bank loaded with pennies in his father's closet.
Like other kids, Di Genova started collecting. Unlike most kids, though, he pursued his adolescent passion for coins and has parlayed it into a successful business as an adult.
"I don't collect myself any longer," he said. "I have such a large percentage of my net worth already on the line, there's no sense having personal assets tied up there, too."
Di Genova, 34, owns Tangible Investments of America Inc., a coin dealership in Laguna Beach, Calif., south of Los Angeles, that he started in 1978.

He brought about half a million dollars worth of coins to a recent interview in New York, to which he wore pleated black-and-white houndstooth slacks, a white shirt and a paisley Versace tie, with the knot loosened.
His love of coins is evident the moment he speaks.

He can describe in detail how Teddy Roosevelt's hiring the renowned sculptor Saint-Gaudens to redesign $20 gold coins led to a national scandal, or name the first year the U.S. Mint made a "double dye" printing error on a penny -- 1955.
He can also quote from memory what the coins are worth.

A Saint-Gaudens with a Roman numeral for the year and details in ultra high relief can bring $100,000, even in low-grade condition. The coins in regular relief will fetch $400 used and up to $10,000 in excellent condition.
A 1955 penny with a blurred or double word from a dye error is worth about $10,000 in superb condition but only several hundred dollars used, he said.
"Condition makes a huge difference. It's true of any collectible but more so in coins and stamps."
It all started when Di Genova was 8, rummaging through his father's closet.
"I found a saltwater taffy cardboard piggy bank that was half-full of pennies. I started going through it and was fascinated. The oldest one was 1918," he said.

His father, an auto body mechanic, had saved the pennies from loose change. Di Genova asked for a blue book to press the coins into. He got one and soon realized how many coins he needed to make a respectable collection. He was hooked.
"As soon as I had a newspaper route, when I was about 10, I was spending all my money on coins," he said. "Very quickly I moved from pennies to like everything."
He took friends on trips to coin shops in central Philadelphia where he met Catherine Bullowa, a dealer who "went out of her way to help young kids get interested in coins."

"We went to 17th and Walnut (Streets) and went looking for pennies, and she had them and she was by far the most reasonable. Some dealers would ask 50 cents or a dollar, and she'd charge a nickel or so."
Bullowa recently won an award for lifetime achievement in coin collecting.

"She would show us different things and she had so much that was priced reasonably. Some of my first great scores were from her," Di Genova said, noting she helped him learn about how to grade coins based on their condition.
Seeing the need for objective standards, Di Genova co-founded the Professional Coin Grading Service in 1976, then later encouraged the establishment of a rival service.
Despite the runup in prices in the 1980s, Di Genova says coins remain a good investment and recommends putting 5 percent of a portfolio in coins as an "insurance policy" against inflation.

Most collectors specialize. You can collect Lincoln pennies, for example, assembling one from each year from each mint where they were made for a complete set. Or you can collect by type -- $5 coins or one of every U.S. coin.

Some people get even more specific, collecting coins based on differences in the dyes used to stamp them. For example, there are 23 varities of the 1832 U.S. Mint half dollar, as catalogued by researcher Al Overton in his book Early Half Dollar Varities (Edward Bros., Ann Arbor, Mich.).

A famous half-dollar is an 1817 coin made with an old recut 1814 dye. The '4' under the '7' is clearly visible on the handful of the coins known, Di Genova said, noting one of them recently fetched about $209,000 at auction.
The history of coin making is filled with such stories that have created thousands of variations for collectors.
You can start sifting through change for old coins but "there's probably not that much there," Di Genova said.
Library books are a good way to learn. Newsletters such as Coin Dealer (310 515-7369) list dealer sales and give a rough idea of wholesale values.
Remember that coin investments are not insured like bank deposits. And while fairly easy to sell, they s.

If you have something that may be valuable, visit at least two or three dealers, preferably those affiliated with the Professional Numismatic Guild or the American Numismatic Association, industry groups that set standards for dealers.
